groupings.title: Hoichi the Earless
groupings.summary: On the quiet shores of Dan-no-ura, a blind musician is summoned to play for a mysterious audience.

posts.title: Hoichi the Earless
posts.summary: A blind musician is summoned to perform before a noble court. But the court is not of the living.

blocks.text: More than seven hundred years ago, in the narrow straits at Dan-no-ura, two great clans met in a final, terrible battle—the Heike and the Genji. By its end, the Heike were destroyed. Warriors, nobles, women, and their young emperor were pulled beneath the waves.

Fishermen still speak of strange lights drifting over the water at night—pale, flickering flames they call oni-bi. When storms roll in, the wind carries a sound like distant battle. And sometimes, in the quiet between waves, there are voices.
A temple was built to soothe the restless dead: Amidaji. Nearby, a cemetery marked the resting place of the fallen.
The dead were never entirely at peace.

In this place lived Hoichi—blind from childhood, trained in the biwa and the recitation of history. His voice was clear, precise, expressive. When he sang of Dan-no-ura, listeners wept. It was said even spirits could not resist his telling.
He had little at first. But the priest of Amidaji took pity on him—a room, food, shelter. In return, Hoichi played on quiet evenings.
Until the night someone came for him.
It was a hot summer night.
The priest had been called away. Unable to sleep in the heavy air, Hoichi sat on the veranda, biwa across his lap, the garden beyond him perfectly still.
They stopped directly in front of him.
I am blind. I cannot see who calls.
There is nothing to fear. My lord — a man of high rank — is staying nearby. He has heard of your skill. You will come with me and perform.
Hoichi rose, took his instrument, and followed.
The grip on his arm was firm — unnaturally so. Metal shifted with each step. Armor. Fully armed.
They moved quickly. Faster than Hoichi thought possible. Soon they passed through a great gate, which opened without a word.
Inside: a garden. Polished floors. Vast rooms.
He was guided to a cushion in a large hall.
You will recite the story of the Battle of Dan-no-ura.

The biwa came alive beneath his hands — oars cutting water, arrows splitting air, ships colliding, steel ringing against steel. His voice carried the rise and fall of battle, the chaos, the grief of inevitable defeat.
Then, softly at first — murmurs. Astonishment.
When he reached the end — the emperor carried under, the last cries of the Heike swallowed by the sea — the hall broke. Not into applause. Into grief. Open, unguarded, inconsolable.
Hoichi faltered. He had moved audiences before. He had never shaken a room like this.
At last, the woman spoke again.
You will return tomorrow night. And the nights that follow.
He was led back before dawn.

sections.title: Part 3 — The Truth in the Dark

blocks.text: Each night Hoichi left. Each morning he returned quieter, his body worn at the edges in a way that sleep did not repair.
Servants were told to follow him.
One night, they did — and lost him almost immediately. He moved through the dark faster than a blind man should move, swallowed by streets they knew well and could not navigate after him.
Then, near the shore, they heard it: the sound of the biwa.
They followed it to the cemetery.
Light from their lanterns fell over the headstones, and they stopped.

Between the grave markers, the air was wrong. Not dark — lit. Dozens of pale flames drifted above the ground, hovering without wind, without source. More than any of them had counted. More than any had seen.
Rain falling around him. Seated before the tomb of the drowned emperor. His voice raised in full performance. His face turned toward nothing.
They seized his shoulders, shouted his name. He fought them.
You must not interrupt — this is an august gathering!
Back to the temple. This time, he told everything.
You have not been visiting a lord's court.
A silence longer than comfort allows.
You have been performing for the dead.
There was only one way to protect him.
Before nightfall, the priest and his assistant covered Hoichi's body in sacred text — sutras written in careful strokes across every surface. Chest, back, face, hands, feet, the backs of his fingers.
These will hide you. Do not speak. Do not move. No matter what you hear.
The figure moved closer. Hoichi heard the shift of armored weight, the soft displacement of air. Felt the presence of something immense and very old leaning over him.
When the voice came again, it was almost to itself:
Something changed in the air. A recognition. A pivot.
The pause that followed had the quality of a held breath.
At dawn, the priest found him where he had been left — seated on the veranda, the floor beneath him dark and wet.
The sutras had covered his body.

People came from distant places to hear him — not just for the skill that had always been extraordinary, but for what that skill had cost. There is something about a man who has been reached for in the dark, and held on, that makes an audience lean in differently.
He lost something he could not get back.
From then on, he was known by a new name:
